sections.overview: The Manumea is a Samoan endemic pigeon now known from the islands of Upolu and Savai‘i, where it persists in very small numbers and is difficult to detect.
sections.identification: Its distinctive heavy bill has tooth-like projections on the lower mandible, an unusual feature among pigeons that gives the species its English name.
sections.habitat: The recovery plan reports it within and along the edges of mature native forest; forest retention is central to the species’ survival.
sections.diet: The French species account reports fruits, including hard fruits of Dysoxylum that the bird can open with its strong bill; detailed dietary studies remain limited.
sections.behavior: Traditional ecological knowledge describes the pigeon as cryptic and difficult to observe, and notes that it may be confused in the field with the Pacific Pigeon.
sections.reproduction: The recovery literature emphasizes major gaps in basic life-history knowledge, so breeding details should be treated as poorly established rather than assumed from other pigeons.
sections.ecology: As the only living species in Didunculus, this forest pigeon represents a distinctive Samoan lineage; its restricted island range makes forest loss and introduced predators especially consequential.
sections.conservation: The IUCN assessment lists it as Critically Endangered; the Samoa recovery plan prioritizes forest protection, invasive-predator management and improved population knowledge.

sources.title: Traditional ecological knowledge of the critically endangered tooth-billed pigeon
